done.why: I sent the robot to grab the crystal sphere, a cage fell on it, and somehow that counted as me dying. I came back at the barrow at the very start. My ruby and pearls went to a cabinet the Wizard keeps under a spell, and everything else went back to the gazebo. Before that I'd already eaten the only shrinking cake without taking the red Evaporate cake, so the pool looked closed to me. Walking the whole way back felt like too much, so I quit.

about: An odd little wizard has stolen the old Empire's treasures and hidden them in caverns south of a ravine, and I'm a returning adventurer trying to get them back. He keeps popping in to cast half-finished spells, like conjuring a fake grue or making me float. The puzzles are mostly about using something on what's around you: luring a dragon to see himself in the ice, answering a riddle, raising a well bucket with water, Alice-style cakes, a robot servant, and a spinning room you have to stop. It's funny and a bit cheeky about itself.

ending.what: I never reached an ending. A death (really the robot's death, though it counted as mine) sent me through the crystal-sphere afterlife and back to the barrow where I started.

moments.note: 'walk toward the glow' wasn't understood. It told me to use compass directions, which I didn't know was a rule.
I asked whether the bridge was safe and a wizard showed up, sized me up, and pretty much told me where the treasure was.
The grue was standing in the light, slightly see-through, and the room was 'embarrassed' about it. Funny.
I reached for a copy of ZORK I and it just vanished. Made me laugh.
I petted the unicorn and it decided I was an uncouth vagabond and left.
'You can't leave the gazebo' even though I'd just walked in. 'go out' worked.
The spinning room sends you somewhere random. It explains why, which helped, but it's still annoying.
'climb into the crack' gave me 'You can't do that!' but 'go up' worked.
The dragon looking at himself in my lamp was a hint I could actually use.
I led the dragon into the ice room. He fought his own reflection, melted the glacier, and died. Very satisfying.
'There's no room' when I put a place mat into an empty metal pan.
I finally found the riddle door, and just typing 'a well' opened it.
The dead dragon had washed up at the ford downstream. The world remembered what I did.
About fifteen turns walking in circles through the spinning room, trying to get back to the riddle room.
I poured the teapot into the bucket and rode up: 'You are at the top of the well. Well done.'
The Wizard showed up again and made me float. I had to wait it out.
'You're holding too many things already!' I had to drop five things to pick up one small cake.
I'd eaten the only green cake. The red one turned out to be 'Evaporate', probably for the pool of tears, and now I can't get small again.
Looking at the cakes through the flask let me read the tiny letters. Clever.
Ordering the robot around and having it press the button that stopped the machinery felt great.
The cage fell on the robot, not me, but I'm the one who 'died' and lost everything. Very confusing.
The face in the mist sent me back to the barrow at the very start, with my treasures locked away.

wished: Ask plain questions like 'what is a grue?' or 'is the bridge safe?' and get some kind of answer instead of 'That sentence isn't one I recognize.'
Walk toward something I can see (the glow, the unicorn) instead of having to know which compass direction it's in.
Have the robot follow me, instead of walking back and forth to give it directions.
Know beforehand that the red cake mattered, or get another green cake, so I could reach the package in the pool.
Not lose everything because the robot died, or at least get some warning about the cage that I understood as a warning.
Talk to the Wizard while he was in the room.

lines.line: It is all south of the ravine, his look says, every treasure the Empire mislaid, and much good may it do you; the pearls nearest, behind a stone door that asks a question
lines.why: It gave me a goal and a direction without spelling everything out.

lines.line: It was never there: the Wizard's word put it in the room, and the room, having no say in the matter, let it, and has the grace to look embarrassed about it now.
lines.why: Funny, and it taught me how the Wizard's spells work.

lines.line: It has that look of a thing that has been through one adventure already and would rather not discuss it.
lines.why: The lamp got a personality. It's what made me feel I could look at everything.

lines.line: he has caught sight of himself in the polished brass of your lamp, and that he does not care for the look of the other dragon in it at all.
lines.why: The hint that cracked the dragon puzzle.

lines.line: There is a muffled explosion and the dragon, a puzzled expression on his face, dies.
lines.why: The best payoff of the session.

lines.line: Whatever it is that makes it go up, it will go up with what is in it and without what is not; that is the whole art of buckets.
lines.why: A big hint, written so it was fun to read.

lines.line: You are at the top of the well. Well done.
Of what you were carrying, the lamp has gone back where you found it and the rest to the gazebo, except the things that were worth anything, which have gone where the Wizard keeps such things
lines.why: This is where I gave up. It was clear about what happened, but losing everything took the wind out of me.

fun.why: The dragon, the bucket and the robot each felt like a real 'aha', and the jokes kept me smiling. It loses a point for the long slog through the spinning room and for the ending that threw me back to the start.

engagement.why: Things kept answering what I did: the dragon washed downstream, the Wizard kept popping in, and the robot actually obeyed me. I wanted to keep going until turn 207 knocked me back.

difficulty.why: The hints in the descriptions were good, but as a newcomer I kept hitting phrasing walls, a random maze room, a carry limit, a one-shot cake I used up, and a robot death that cost me everything.

interestingness.why: Clever puzzles, a mischievous wizard who keeps intruding, and a world that remembers what you did. Every room had something to poke at.

prose.why: Dry and witty, and the hints are tucked into jokes instead of signposts. The lamp, the embarrassed room and the bucket lines were a pleasure to read.
